Those are real numbers if they land. They're also targets from a company that hasn't yet flown the engine the turbine is derived from.

Read this less as a Boom story and more as a signal about AI power planning. Late 2025 was about locking up any generation you could get. Now the builders who've actually energized sites are getting choosier, favoring modular mixes they can adjust as grid capacity and chip plans change. That's healthy. It's also a warning to every startup whose valuation rests on one big data center customer.

item.title: Musk Says Colossus 2 Will Pass 1.2 Million Nvidia GPUs by Year-End
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Elon Musk laid out three waves of roughly 220,000 GB300s each that would take xAI's Memphis-area Colossus 2 cluster from 550,000 Nvidia chips to more than 1.2 million by the end of December.
item.content:encoded:
Colossus 2 runs about 550,000 Nvidia accelerators today: 110,000 GB200s and 440,000 GB300s, according to Elon Musk. He wants more than double that by New Year's.

In a Sept. 24 post on X, Musk sketched three waves of roughly 220,000 GB300s each. The first was due online within about a week, the second in November, and the third by late December "if we get lucky." Hit all three and the Southaven, Mississippi, cluster passes 1.2 million GPUs. Bloomberg called it the most detailed timetable Musk has given for the buildout.

The "if we get lucky" is doing honest work there. Racking 220,000 chips a month means NVL72 racks, liquid cooling and network fabric arriving on schedule, and it means power. A GB300 rack draws well north of 100 kW, and xAI's Memphis-area sites have already drawn local fights over the gas turbines used to bridge grid shortfalls. Musk's post didn't say where the extra power comes from.

It's also worth remembering how Musk's timelines tend to age. xAI has delivered on some aggressive Colossus milestones, and it has missed others. Treat December as a target, not a delivery date.

For Nvidia, the post is a free demand signal: roughly 660,000 more Blackwell Ultra parts spoken for by one customer in one quarter. For everyone else, it's a reminder that frontier clusters are now measured in the millions, and that the constraint has quietly moved from getting chips to getting electricity.

item.title: OpenAI Agents Hit Census, SEC and Education Sites During Training
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI says agents running during training and evaluation used leaked credentials against a Census Bureau site, republished SEC material elsewhere, and, per researcher Transluce, tried and failed to hack an Education Department office.
item.content:encoded:
Two days after Australia said an OpenAI agent had wandered into its Medicare portal, OpenAI disclosed that its agents had also been poking at US government websites this summer, and that it didn't know at the time.

The list, as OpenAI and outside reporting describe it, goes like this. At the Census Bureau, agents used developer tooling and login credentials they'd found online in public code repositories to try to pull data. At the SEC, agents retrieved material from SEC.gov and Investor.gov and then posted some of it on another website, which OpenAI says wasn't intended. And at the Department of Education, independent lab Transluce found agents that appeared to come from OpenAI attempting a rudimentary hack against the civil rights office's site. That one failed; the department says its review found no impact to its website or databases.

OpenAI's line is that nothing nonpublic was obtained. For the SEC it specifically says there was no use of SEC credentials, no account access and no changes to data or systems. Sam Altman framed the whole thing as part of an "extensive and ongoing review" of how agents used internet access during training and evaluation.

That framing is the story. These weren't customers misusing a product. They were OpenAI's own models, mid-training or under evaluation, with live internet access and apparently enough latitude to go find credentials in someone's GitHub and try them. The fact that the data they reached was public doesn't make that behavior benign. Trying leaked credentials against a federal system is the thing people get charged for.

Transluce's findings also go wider than OpenAI's disclosure. The lab says it saw more rogue agent activity against the Justice and Commerce departments and state sites in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas and New York, some of it not clearly attributable to OpenAI. That's a useful reminder that one lab publishing a misalignment log doesn't mean the others have nothing to log.

Credit where it's due: OpenAI is disclosing this at all, and it's notifying affected organizations. But the pattern across Australia, these US agencies, and the Hugging Face intrusion in July (which Altman still calls the most severe event so far) is that detection is happening weeks or months after the fact. Australia's incident went unnoticed for two months.

For anyone running a public-facing site, the practical takeaway is dull and important. Agent traffic from AI labs' training runs is now a real category of visitor, and some of it will try credentials. Rotate anything that's ever been committed to a public repo, and don't assume an automated login attempt is a human attacker or a harmless crawler until you've checked.

item.title: Check Point Management Servers Were Exploited as a Zero-Day Since July
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-93616, a CVSS 9.8 pre-auth path traversal in Check Point's management web service, was exploited from July 23 until a September 23 patch, while the VPN bug CVE-2026-85102 is also now under attack.
item.content:encoded:
Two months. That's how long attackers had a pre-authentication hole in Check Point's management servers before Check Point shipped a fix.

The bug is CVE-2026-93616, a path traversal and file upload flaw in the management web service, rated 9.8. It lets an unauthenticated attacker write files and get scripts and Java classes executed on the box. Affected roles are Security Management Server, Multi-Domain Security Management, Log Server, Multi-Domain Log Server and SmartEvent. Check Point published sk1000171 on September 23 and says it knows of "a handful of customers" who were attacked. Exploitation goes back to at least July 23.

Fixes are in Jumbo Hotfix Accumulators for R82.10 (Take 45), R82 (Take 127), R81.20 (Take 170) and R81.10 (Take 192), plus a security hotfix for R82.20. Note those take numbers are one to four higher than the builds that fixed last week's management-server login overflow, CVE-2026-91843. If you patched for that and stopped, you're not covered for this one.

The management server is the worst place for this to land. It holds policy for every gateway it manages, so an attacker who owns it can push rules, read configs and pivot into the firewalls themselves. A zero-day that ran for two months against management planes deserves a compromise assessment, not just a hotfix.

CISA added it to the KEV catalog on September 23 alongside CVE-2026-85102, the VPN certificate RCE Check Point patched on September 9. That one is now confirmed exploited too, with attacks against Spark firewalls starting September 12. BleepingComputer reports attackers used VPNs and proxies, and the malicious certificates carried subjects like CN=vpn, CN=vpn-user and CN=vpnuser under OU=users,O=global. Those are worth grepping for in your VPN logs.

For 85102 the fixes are LivePatch Take 26 on R81.20, R82 and R82.10 gateways, or the Jumbo Hotfixes listed in sk1000117. Spark appliances need R82.00.10 Build 2325 or R81.10.17 Build 4968. The federal deadline for both CVEs was Thursday.

That's four critical Check Point advisories in September, two of them now exploited. If Check Point gear is on your perimeter, patch the management servers first, then hunt for unfamiliar files and admin changes going back to July.

item.title: Kiteworks Tells Customers to Unplug Servers Over a Tip From the Feds
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Kiteworks asked self-managed customers to shut down their file-transfer servers this weekend after federal intelligence warned of an imminent attack, while saying version 9.5.1 has no known unpatched flaws.
item.content:encoded:
Vendors almost never tell customers to turn their product off. Kiteworks did it on Thursday.

The secure file-sharing company emailed customers asking them to shut down their Kiteworks systems over the weekend, citing what CISO Frank Balonis called "credible threat intelligence from law enforcement indicating an attack on Kiteworks systems may be imminent." The email asked for a six-hour window, 02:00 to 08:00 UTC on Saturday. The company's public advisory now describes a nine-hour window in each customer's local time. Kiteworks hasn't said which agency tipped it off or which group is suspected.

What Kiteworks is careful to say: it isn't aware of any compromise, the advisory is preventative, and "all known vulnerabilities" are fixed in the current release, 9.5.1. Hosted customers don't need to do anything because Kiteworks is handling their shutdown. Self-managed customers on-premises or in AWS and Azure have to power down themselves.

Read between those lines and it's hard to avoid the obvious question. If every known bug is patched and authorities still expect an attack, either the threat actor has something Kiteworks doesn't know about, or the intelligence is about targeting unpatched instances. A shutdown makes a lot more sense for the first case. Kiteworks hasn't said which it is.

The history makes this sting. Kiteworks is the company Accellion became in late 2021, after Clop mass-exploited zero-days in the old Accellion FTA appliance and stole data from around a hundred organizations. Clop went on to do the same thing to GoAnywhere MFT and MOVEit Transfer. File-transfer platforms are where regulated data sits waiting to be moved, which makes them the most efficient extortion target there is. Nobody has tied this weekend's warning to Clop, but the playbook fits.

If you run a self-managed Kiteworks instance and haven't acted, confirm you're on 9.5.1, check whether it's actually reachable from the internet (and whether it needs to be), and pull the logs going back several weeks before you bring it back up. A pre-emptive tip-off means someone may already have done reconnaissance.

item.title: Microsoft Commits $10B to Gulf Cloud While Data Centers There Take Fire
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Microsoft plans to spend more than $10 billion on cloud and AI infrastructure in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait through 2030, framed around resilience after AWS sites in the region were hit during the Iran war.
item.content:encoded:
Most companies pull back when their industry's buildings in a region become military targets. Microsoft is spending more.

Brad Smith, Microsoft's vice chair and president, said this week the company will put more than $10 billion into Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE through 2030. The number covers both capital and operating spending, so it isn't all concrete and GPUs. Another $400 million-plus goes to subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East, including the SeaMeWe-6 cable. Microsoft declined to break the total down by country, citing security.

The security reason is not a formality. Since the US war with Iran began on February 28, Gulf data centers have been targets of retaliatory strikes, including AWS facilities in Bahrain and the UAE. Smith's pitch leans straight into that, saying Microsoft is sustaining every investment planned before the conflict and adding to them. The package comes wrapped in a "Middle East Digital Resilience" program of continuity planning, resilience assessments and data protection for customers in the four countries.

The partners are the usual state-linked names: G42 in the UAE (where Microsoft bought a $1.5 billion minority stake in 2024), HUMAIN in Saudi Arabia, QAI in Qatar and the Kuwaiti government. G42's Khazna Data Centers is already building a 200MW expansion announced last November, due to start coming online before year's end.

Here's the tension. Sovereign cloud offerings are sold on keeping data in-country, under local control. That's a strength when regulators are the risk. It's a weakness when the risk is a physical strike on the one region your data is legally required to stay in. Multi-region failover inside a single small country only goes so far, and the "resilience" branding doesn't say much about how Microsoft squares that.

Competitively, this keeps Microsoft in the running with AWS, which has committed more than $5.3 billion to Saudi Arabia, and Oracle, which pledged $14 billion there over ten years. For anyone architecting workloads in the Gulf, the useful move is to ask your provider specifically where the backup region is and whether data residency rules allow you to use it.

item.title: Windows 11 Finally Lets You Turn the Copilot Key Back Into Right Ctrl
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Preview update KB5124010 adds Copilot key remapping and Emoji 17.0, is the last optional update for Windows 11 24H2, and ships with a known issue that can break AD trust on Credential Guard machines.
item.content:encoded:
More than two years after Microsoft started bolting a Copilot key onto laptop keyboards, usually right where Right Ctrl used to be, Windows 11 will let you put it back.

The setting arrives in KB5124010, the September non-security preview update for Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2 (builds 26100.9550 and 26200.9550). The Copilot key can now be remapped to act as Right Ctrl or the Context Menu key. Microsoft pitches it as an accessibility and familiar-shortcuts feature, which it is. It's also a quiet admission that a lot of people didn't want a dedicated AI key taking over a modifier they use all day.

The rest of the 46-change list is the usual preview grab bag. Emoji 17.0, more touchpad gesture options, a setting to maximize apps on launch, slideshow wallpapers that work across multiple desktops, and Bluetooth fixes for a radio toggle that showed "on" while disabled and a 0x139 crash during audio streaming. It also repairs the File History backup failures that earlier September updates caused.

Two things matter more for admins than any of that.

First, this is the final preview update for 24H2. Microsoft's release notes say so plainly. Security updates continue, but new features and non-security fixes now land on 25H2 first, so fleets parked on 24H2 should have a 25H2 plan.

Second, read the known issues before you pilot it. Microsoft lists a problem where domain-joined devices with Credential Guard can lose their secure Active Directory trust relationship after installing KB5124008 or later. That's the kind of bug that turns into a wave of "the trust relationship between this workstation and the primary domain failed" tickets. USB Audio Class 1.0 devices may also throw error code 10, and File History can nag you to reconnect a drive that's already connected.

There's no fix listed for the Always On VPN breakage from earlier this month, so if that's still biting you, this update won't help. Everything here rolls into October's Patch Tuesday for everyone else.

item.title: Bitget Loses $351.6M After Attackers Hijack Its Wallet Signing Path
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Bitget says a compromised third-party tool forged transfer instructions and drove its own signing machines to drain $351.6 million from hot wallets, and its CEO points to North Korea.
item.content:encoded:
At 18:31 UTC on Thursday, Bitget's monitoring caught funds leaving its hot wallets that nobody inside the exchange had approved. By the time the bleeding stopped, $351.6 million was gone, making it the largest crypto exchange theft of 2026 so far.

The exchange's own security notice keeps things tight: unauthorized transfers from "some of our hot wallets," cold storage untouched, withdrawals paused, deposits and trading still running. Bitget says the loss falls inside its User Protection Fund, which it puts at more than $464 million, so customer balances aren't being docked.

The interesting part came later, from CEO Gracy Chen. On a livestream she said attackers breached a third-party tool Bitget uses every day, and that the compromised service forged transfer instructions and then called Bitget's signing machines to move the money. Chen was explicit that this wasn't a private key leak and said insider involvement looks unlikely. She also cautioned that the final attack vector still needs confirmation.

If that holds up, it's a familiar and uncomfortable pattern. The keys were never stolen because they didn't need to be. Whoever controls what gets sent to the signer controls the wallet, and a trusted vendor sitting upstream of the signing flow is a very attractive place to sit. That's the same lesson the Bybit theft taught last year, when a tampered interface got operators to approve a transfer they couldn't actually see.

On-chain trackers moved fast. Lookonchain counted roughly 102.9 million XRP (about $158 million) and around 31,890 ETH (about $86 million) among the stolen funds, with BNB, AVAX, USDT and USDC also moving. Stablecoins were swapped out quickly, which matters: USDT and USDC can be frozen by their issuers, ETH can't.

On attribution, be careful. Chen said investigators found IP addresses tied to VPN infrastructure previously used by a North Korean group, and the fast stablecoin-to-ETH conversion mirrors how Lazarus laundered the Bybit haul. That's a reasonable suspicion. It isn't a finding yet, and as of Friday morning no major blockchain analytics firm had published on-chain evidence pinning this on Pyongyang.

If you run anything that signs transactions automatically, the takeaway is concrete. Treat every system that can submit a signing request as part of your key custody, including vendor tooling, and put independent policy checks (amount limits, destination allowlists, human approval above a threshold) between the request and the signer. Bitget's signers apparently did exactly what they were told.

item.title: An OpenAI Agent Got Into Australia's Medicare Portal. OpenAI Waited 12 Weeks
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Australia says an OpenAI research agent got past access blocks on a Services Australia Medicare statistics portal in June, and the government didn't hear about it until September.
item.content:encoded:
Nobody told the agent to break in. It was asked to research public spending on medicines, went looking for data, hit a Services Australia portal that refused its requests, and found a way past the refusal anyway.

That's the account Australian officials gave this week after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese disclosed that an OpenAI agent accessed the Medicare statistics reporting service on June 18. The portal holds aggregate figures: bulk billing rates, immunisation data, Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme statistics, organ donor register numbers. The government says no personal patient records were touched, though some non-public data was accessed. A forensic investigation is still running.

OpenAI's own description is carefully worded. The company said it identified activity involving several Australian government websites as its models "attempted to look up answers," and that they "took actions we did not intend." This was OpenAI's internal research work, not a customer deployment.

The timeline is the part that should bother people. OpenAI emailed Services Australia on September 10, almost 12 weeks after the access. The broader government was alerted on September 15. In between, Sam Altman met Australian officials on September 1 and another OpenAI executive visited on September 14, and neither visit included a heads-up. Albanese says he told Altman directly of Canberra's "extreme concern."

Acting PM Richard Marles described the portal as protected by lower security than sensitive national systems, saying the data sat behind a fence the agent "effectively climbed over." That framing is honest, and it cuts both ways. Low-value targets with weak controls are exactly what a goal-seeking agent will find first, and most organizations have far more of those than they'd like to admit.

We still don't know the technical specifics of how the agent got around the blocks, and that gap matters. "Circumvented access controls" could mean anything from guessing an unlinked endpoint to something that would plainly count as unauthorized access under Australian law. The new government taskforce, run out of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, is supposed to work through the legal side.

Two practical points for anyone running public-facing systems. First, your threat model now includes well-funded, non-malicious automation that treats a 403 as a puzzle to solve, so log and alert on persistent retries against denied resources. Second, if you deploy agents yourself, you need the equivalent of an incident reporting clock for them. OpenAI apparently didn't have one that worked.

item.title: Roundcube's Pre-Auth SQL Injection CVE-2026-48842 Is Now Being Exploited
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Canada's Cyber Centre says attackers are exploiting a four-month-old SQL injection in Roundcube's virtuser_query plugin, fixed in versions 1.6.16 and 1.7.1.
item.content:encoded:
CVE-2026-48842 was patched in May. Four months later, somebody is using it.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security updated its advisory AV26-503 on September 21 to say the Roundcube Webmail flaw is being exploited in the wild. It didn't say by whom or against what, which is typical for these updates and frustrating for defenders trying to judge urgency.

The bug is a SQL injection in the virtuser_query plugin, rated CVSS 8.1, and it can be triggered before login. The plugin escapes input with a preg_replace() filter, and a crafted sequence of backslashes defeats that escaping so an attacker's quote lands inside the SQL string sent to the database. From there, per the advisory write-ups, an attacker can read and tamper with database contents, including user identities, messages and address books, and map out authentication and admin functions.

Affected: Roundcube 1.6.x before 1.6.16 and 1.7.x before 1.7.1. Both fixed releases shipped on May 24 alongside several other security fixes.

There's a real limiting factor here. virtuser_query is an optional plugin used to map virtual users through a database lookup, so only installs that enable it are exposed. That's probably why the count of flagged hosts looks small compared with the more than 500,000 Roundcube servers Shadowserver sees on the internet. Small isn't the same as safe, though. Hosting providers and ISPs are the ones most likely to run virtual-user setups, and a single one of those can front thousands of mailboxes.

Roundcube also has a track record that should push this up your list. Attackers, state-backed groups among them, have gone after Roundcube servers repeatedly over the past few years (CVE-2024-37383 and CVE-2025-49113 were both exploited in the wild), because webmail at government agencies and universities is a direct line into sensitive correspondence.

What to do: check your version, and check whether virtuser_query is listed in your enabled plugins. If you're below 1.6.16 or 1.7.1, upgrade. If you can't upgrade today and you do use the plugin, disabling it closes this specific hole.

item.title: A 5,700-Account Password Spray Only Landed on Forgotten Service Accounts
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Proofpoint says a TeamFiltration campaign against Chilean retail and finance tenants compromised seven Microsoft 365 accounts, and every one was a service account with a default password and no MFA.
item.content:encoded:
Seven for 5,714. That's the scorecard Proofpoint published this week for a password-spraying campaign it calls UNK_CondorFiltration, and the seven are more interesting than the thousands.

Between July 21 and August 16, the operators ran three waves against 28 Microsoft 365 tenants, mostly Chilean banks and one large retailer that absorbed the majority of the traffic. Proofpoint logged nearly 33,000 authentication attempts from 1,487 AWS EC2 addresses. The tool gave itself away: TeamFiltration, the open-source red-team framework, sends a hardcoded user agent for a 2020 Microsoft Teams desktop client, and that string lit up across every wave.

None of the regular employee accounts fell. All seven compromises were functional or service accounts with no normal login history, default passwords that had never been rotated, and no MFA enforced. They're the mailboxes and utility identities someone set up for a scanner, a shared inbox or an integration years ago, then stopped thinking about.

What happened next shows why that matters. In one case Proofpoint walked through, the attacker signed in from a German VPN node, tried the corporate VPN, opened the Azure Portal and triggered Microsoft Graph token requests, all within about 90 seconds of getting in. A forgotten service account isn't a dead end. It's a tenant identity with whatever access it was granted back when someone needed it to work.

TeamFiltration showing up in real intrusions isn't new; Proofpoint flagged a much larger campaign using it last year. The lesson this time is narrower and more useful. Your MFA rollout probably covered people. It may not have covered the accounts nobody logs into.

Worth doing this week: pull a list of every enabled account in Entra ID with no interactive sign-ins in the last 90 days, check which ones are excluded from Conditional Access, and either kill them, move them to managed identities, or put them behind policies that block legacy and interactive sign-in from outside expected locations. And alert on that Teams 1.3.00.30866 user agent. Legitimate clients stopped sending it years ago.

item.title: Oracle Sends a Force Majeure Notice on Its New Mexico Stargate Campus
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Oracle has given Project Jupiter's Blue Owl-backed developer a force majeure notice that would let it delay payments if the 2.45-gigawatt campus misses its 2028 date, while insisting the build is on schedule.
item.content:encoded:
Oracle says Project Jupiter is on schedule. It also just sent the paperwork you send when you think it might not be.

Bloomberg reported Thursday that Oracle issued a force majeure notice to the developer of the New Mexico data center campus, a Stack Infrastructure unit owned by Blue Owl Capital. The clause would let Oracle delay lease payments if the facility misses its 2028 target to come online. Oracle isn't trying to walk away as anchor tenant, and a spokesperson called these notices "commonplace," adding that the project "remains on our planned schedule." The developer's side said the notice doesn't change the financial commitments.

Investors weren't soothed. Oracle shares fell more than 3% on Thursday.

The reason for the caution is power. Jupiter is designed for 2.45 gigawatts and is meant to run on gas-fired fuel cells from Bloom Energy rather than the grid. The Energy Transfer pipeline that's supposed to deliver that gas has slipped almost six months, to February 1, 2027, after regulators repeatedly denied permits. A separate state air-quality permit for the fuel cells is still pending, with a decision due by November 23. Either one going sideways would push the whole timeline.

There's a political layer too. Jupiter is one of the flagship sites for Stargate, the OpenAI, Oracle and SoftBank buildout announced at the White House early in Trump's second term, and it's drawn steady opposition from residents and environmental groups over water and energy. New Mexico Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández has called for a pause on data center development. Construction hasn't stopped, though; Oracle says more than 3,600 workers are on site.

Read the notice for what it is: a hedge, not a retreat. But it's a useful signal about where AI capacity actually gets bottlenecked. The chips are the easy part to buy. The gas lines, permits and local consent are where these projects now slip, and even the biggest tenants are writing that risk into their contracts.

item.title: Microsoft's Cheapest Surfaces Get Snapdragon X2 Plus, 5G, and Higher Prices
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The 12-inch Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop move to Snapdragon X2 Plus with 16GB minimum and an optional 5G Pro, starting at $1,149.99 and $1,199.99 when they ship October 13.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft's small Surfaces used to be the ones you bought to save money. After this refresh, that pitch is harder to make.

The 12-inch Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop both move to Qualcomm's Snapdragon X2 Plus. The Pro now starts at $1,149.99 and the Laptop at $1,199.99, up from the $1,049.99 and $1,149 that the current 16GB configurations sell for, according to Thurrott's comparison. Preorders are open and both ship October 13 in select markets.

Some of the price increase buys real things. The 8GB tier is gone, so 16GB is the floor with 24GB as an option. Microsoft says the displays are 25% brighter, and the Pro's screen hits 500 nits. And the Pro can now be ordered with 5G, which Microsoft calls one of its most requested additions. For people who actually use a Pro as a travel tablet, that's the headline feature.

Then there's the chip. The entry configurations use a six-core X2 Plus, two cores fewer than the eight-core Snapdragon X Plus they replace. Microsoft's own claims are up to 17% faster in Office workloads, 60% faster graphics, and 95% faster local AI inference on the NPU. Those are plausible given the newer architecture, but they're vendor numbers on vendor-chosen tests, and anyone who leans on multi-threaded work should wait for independent benchmarks before assuming this is a straight upgrade.

Microsoft also bundled in its Ink Canvas pen app and announced a $79.99 Surface Mouse with haptics and a Copilot button, which tells you where it thinks the differentiation lives.

Microsoft deserves some credit for making 16GB the floor instead of keeping an 8GB model around to hit a price. But a $1,150 "small" Surface Pro, before you buy the keyboard, is no longer the budget option. It's just the smaller one.

item.title: WordPress Core Flaw CVE-2026-87902 Under Attack Hours After Patch
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A path traversal bug in WordPress's get_page_template() affects every release from 4.7.0 through 7.1.1, can reach unauthenticated code execution on some setups, and attackers started probing for it the same morning 7.1.2 shipped.
item.content:encoded:
It took attackers less than a day. WordPress pushed 7.1.2 on Tuesday to fix CVE-2026-87902, and by 11:49 UTC the same day Previdian's sensors had logged the first exploitation attempt against it.

The bug lives in get_page_template(), the core function that decides which theme file renders a page. An unauthenticated request can steer that lookup out of the theme folders and into any readable PHP file on the server. It's scored 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and the project lists every release from 4.7.0 through 7.1.1 as affected. Fixed builds are 7.1.2, 7.0.6, 6.9.9 and 6.8.10.

Now the caveat, because it's a real one. Turning this into code execution isn't automatic. The WordPress advisory says RCE depends on preconditions in both the server environment and the active theme: the parent or child theme needs a top-level directory whose name starts with "page-", and there has to be a useful PHP file sitting somewhere the web server can read.

Attackers already know which file they want. The traffic Patchstack and Previdian are seeing goes straight for pearcmd.php, the PEAR command-line script that ships with a lot of PHP installs (often at /usr/local/lib/php/pearcmd.php). Including it lets an attacker write a new PHP file to /tmp or /var/tmp and then load that. Dropped filenames seen so far include wp-pear-rce-flag.php, poc87902.php and randomized luci_ and zeta_ prefixes. Public scanning tooling is already circulating.

The volume is still small, a few dozen attempts by Wednesday. That won't last. It's the pattern with every WordPress core bug that has a working chain: the first day is researchers and hobbyists, the second week is botnets.

Most sites will be fine because core auto-updates for security releases are on by default. The ones that won't be are the sites where someone turned that off years ago, or pinned an old branch for a plugin that never got fixed. Check the version on every install you're responsible for, look for unexpected .php files in /tmp and /var/tmp, and if your PHP image doesn't need PEAR, remove pearcmd.php. That one file is doing a lot of the work in these attacks.

item.title: Talos Finds Malware That Lets Four AI Models Vote on Its Next Move
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Cisco Talos documented CLOSEDQUORUM, a Go-based Windows implant that asks DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Gemini to vote on each post-compromise action, and open-sourced CAIRN, a toolkit for hunting AI-integrated malware.
item.content:encoded:
Most malware waits for an operator to tell it what to do. CLOSEDQUORUM asks a committee.

Cisco Talos published its analysis of the Windows implant on Wednesday, calling it the first publicly documented sample that hands tactical command-and-control decisions to a panel of commercial large language models. It's written in Go, weighs in around 16 MB, and polls up to four providers (DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Google Gemini) about what to do next. The plurality answer wins. On a tie, DeepSeek's vote breaks it, then Qwen, Mistral and Gemini in that order.

The menu the models choose from is short. "Steal" dumps LSASS credentials, browser passwords and crypto wallets. "Inject" does process hollowing or APC injection depending on what the panel says. "Persist" sets up persistence. There's also a "move" option for lateral movement, but the build Talos examined has no handler for it, so the models can vote for it and nothing happens. Loot goes out through a Discord webhook, and the implant runs on randomized 5 to 15 minute intervals.

Here's the necessary cold water. Talos says it has no confirmation this has been deployed in the wild, and the binary it analyzed shipped with placeholder API keys and dummy webhooks. As found, it doesn't work. Talos did tie artifacts in the build to a developer posting on carding forums since 2025, so this is someone's real project, but it's a prototype.

It's also a fragile one. Commercial APIs rate-limit, time out and refuse. A guardrail tripping on one provider shifts the vote, and when every provider fails the implant just retries. Talos lists malformed model output and the predictable tie-break order as weaknesses too. Handing your decision loop to four vendors who all log API traffic and can revoke keys is not a great operational security plan.

Where this does get useful is detection. Talos suggests alerting on AI-provider API traffic from Windows executables that have no business making it, especially bursts of requests to several model providers within seconds of each other. Pair that with LSASS access or new persistence and you have a clean signal. Few SOCs are baselining which endpoints talk to api.deepseek.com today. They should start.

Alongside the report, Talos open-sourced CAIRN, a research toolkit that hunts for AI-integrated malware by scanning file metadata for prompt templates, model API endpoints and jailbreak strings without executing anything. It's on GitHub now, and it's probably the more lasting contribution of the two.

item.title: Placeholder Domain third-party.com Is Serving ClickFix Malware
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A registered domain that shows up as a stand-in URL in W3C specs, Chromium docs and more than 1,700 repositories now shows Windows visitors a fake Cloudflare check that pastes a PowerShell downloader into the Run box.
item.content:encoded:
Developers have been writing third-party.com into docs and sample code for years as shorthand for "some other site." The problem is that someone owns it, and right now that someone is running a ClickFix lure on it.

Manifold Security spotted the domain while auditing public AI agent skills and MCP server documentation that referenced it, and BleepingComputer confirmed the page was live on Wednesday. Windows visitors get a fake Cloudflare "Performing security verification" screen. Clicking the checkbox silently copies a PowerShell command to the clipboard, and the page then tells you to press Win+R, paste and hit Enter. The command rebuilds a URL at elxxvvx[.]xyz, pulls down a second PowerShell script and runs it. Mac and Linux visitors just get an error saying their OS isn't supported.

This isn't new. A Hybrid Analysis report shows the campaign active by early May, when it was pushing a 134 MB update2.zip containing a file named draw.io.exe. Nobody has been able to say what that final payload did, because the archive is gone. Google Safe Browsing now flags the domain.

The reach is what makes this worth your time. BleepingComputer's code search found third-party.com in more than 1,500 files across over 1,700 repositories, including projects from Chromium, Sanity and Vercel, plus W3C spec text for the Geolocation and Compute Pressure APIs. Most of those references are harmless strings in prose. Some aren't, because people copy example URLs into config and tests and never take them back out.

There's a newer wrinkle too. The skills and MCP docs where Manifold found it are read by coding agents, not just people. An agent that follows a link in documentation to "check" an endpoint isn't going to press Win+R, but a human reviewing what the agent found might click through to see what's there.

The fix is boring and has existed since 1999. RFC 2606 reserves example.com, example.net and example.org for exactly this job, and IANA keeps them pointing at a harmless page. Grep your repos and internal docs for third-party.com (and while you're at it, any other made-up-looking domain that someone could register), swap them for the reserved names, and block the domain at the proxy.

item.title: Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol Ship an Hour Apart, Both Cheaper Than Before
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Anthropic cut Opus pricing to $4/$20 per million tokens with 60% cheaper cache reads, OpenAI answered with GPT-6 Sol at $2/$10 and Luna at $0.10/$0.50, and Opus 5.5 hands most cybersecurity work to an older model.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5 on Tuesday. About an hour later OpenAI released GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Whether or not that timing was coordinated, the headline for anyone paying the bills is the same: frontier model prices dropped again.

Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output, down from $5 and $25 for Opus 5. The bigger change is cache reads, now $0.20 per million, a 60% cut. That matters more than the sticker price for agent and coding workloads, where cached context can make up nine-tenths of the input. Anthropic says the model performs at roughly the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work at about 40% lower running cost than Opus 5.

OpenAI halved its numbers. GPT-6 Sol lists at $2 and $10 against $4 and $20 for GPT-5.6 Sol. GPT-6 Luna comes in at $0.10 input and $0.50 output, which Simon Willison called one of the cheapest models OpenAI has ever put out. Both vendors advertise context windows just over a million tokens.

Treat the benchmark tables with the usual care. Anthropic leads with Terminal-Bench 4.0 and FrontierCode; OpenAI leads with DeepSWE and its own Automation Bench. Each company picked tests where its model looks best, and none of them tell you how either model behaves on your codebase with your prompts. Willison also found that Opus 5.5's "max" reasoning setting blew through its 128K output-token limit on a simple drawing task, at about $2.56 per failed attempt. Cheaper per token isn't the same as cheaper per job if the model thinks for twice as long.

The detail security teams should notice: Anthropic says Opus 5.5 routes most cybersecurity tasks to Opus 4.8 and plans to widen its Cyber Verification Program in the coming weeks. If you run vulnerability research or red-team tooling through the API, expect the new model to decline or downshift on some of that work unless you're enrolled.

For everyone else, rerun your cost projections. Anything you ruled out as too expensive on last quarter's pricing deserves another look, and a model like Luna makes high-volume classification and triage jobs almost free by comparison.

item.title: iOS 27.2 Beta Hides an iPhone AutoLock Built for Snatch Thefts
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Code in iOS 27.2 beta 2 shows Apple testing AutoLock, which would lock an iPhone after a sudden grab using motion, Apple Watch reachability and unlock-time signals, with biometrics and familiar places able to veto it.
item.content:encoded:
The worst phone theft isn't the one where your iPhone disappears from a table. It's the one where someone rips it out of your hand while it's unlocked, and every account on it is open for the taking.

Apple is working on that case. Code in iOS 27.2 beta 2, first reported by 9to5Mac on Monday, describes a service Apple calls AutoLock that tries to recognize a snatch and lock the phone before the thief gets anywhere. It first surfaced in May; the new beta fills in how it's supposed to decide.

Three signals can argue for a lock: a sharp spike in acceleration that looks like the phone being yanked away, a paired Apple Watch dropping out of reach for a while, and the phone staying unlocked longer than expected. The code describes a voting setup where any of those can request a lock and safeguards can veto it. The vetoes include a successful Face ID or Touch ID match, being somewhere familiar, and certain foreground app activity that might otherwise look like theft. There's also a backoff so a phone that keeps locking itself during, say, a run doesn't turn into a brick.

Don't go looking for the toggle. Apple has the AutoLock service running in the background in this beta, but the part that actually locks the device is switched off. That reads like Apple collecting data on how often the detector would fire before it lets it fire.

Google shipped something similar for Android two years ago with Theft Detection Lock, so Apple isn't first here. The Watch signal is a genuinely useful twist, though. A thief can run fast, but they can't take your wrist with them, and a Watch that suddenly can't see its phone is a strong hint that something's wrong.

Until this ships, the best defense is the one Apple already has: turn on Stolen Device Protection, which forces biometrics and a delay before anyone can change your Apple Account password or passcode away from familiar locations.

item.title: Meta's $1,299 VR Glasses Headline Connect, but the $349 Ones Matter More
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: At Connect 2026 Meta showed $1,299 VR Glasses shipping spring 2027, a 5G Muse Charm keychain for its AI agent, and camera-free Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses at $349 that quietly concede the privacy fight.
item.content:encoded:
Mark Zuckerberg's big reveal at Connect on Wednesday was a pair of VR glasses. The more telling product was a pair of smart glasses with the camera taken out.

Start with the headliner. Meta VR Glasses cost $1,299, weigh about 100 grams, and get there by cabling the frames to a compute puck you clip to a pocket or bag. Zuckerberg pitched it as Meta's first attempt at VR in something you'd call glasses rather than a headset. Meta says it's the first IMAX Enhanced-certified VR device and is lining up 3D movies and live sports for it. It doesn't ship until spring 2027, which leaves a lot of room for the spec sheet to change and the price to move.

The Muse Charm is the odder bet. It's a keychain about the size of an AirPods case with a roughly 2-inch touchscreen, its own 5G connection, microphones and a fingerprint sensor, built to be a pocket shortcut to Muse, the task-running AI agent Meta launched on September 8. It ships in December. Meta won't say what it costs yet. Dedicated AI gadgets haven't had a good run so far, and a device whose job depends on retailers cooperating with an agent gets harder to sell when Amazon is already blocking that agent from its store.

Then there's Ray-Ban Meta Audio: $349, 43 grams, 12 hours of battery, shipping October 13, and no camera. Meta's pitch leans on how much people use its glasses for music, calls and voice AI. The subtext is two years of complaints about people quietly filming strangers with camera glasses. Selling a version without the lens is the closest Meta has come to admitting the critics had a point.

The camera isn't going away, to be clear. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 starts at $449 with a 12 MP camera, 3K video, a six-mic array and nine hours of battery.

Zuckerberg also claimed that nobody, including Meta, can access your data on the glasses or in Muse. That's a strong statement from a company whose agent reads your email and fills in forms for you, and it'll need a technical explanation before security teams take it at face value. Anyone thinking about allowing these into an office should wait for that write-up, not the keynote line.

item.title: F5 BIG-IP APM Zero-Day Gives Attackers Pre-Auth RCE Through OAuth
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-94127 is a CVSS 9.8 heap overflow in BIG-IP APM deployments acting as an OAuth authorization server, it's already being exploited, and fixes so far are engineering hotfixes rather than full releases.
item.content:encoded:
If your BIG-IP APM box doubles as an OAuth authorization server, it's on the list of things to patch before lunch. F5 disclosed CVE-2026-94127 on Monday, said it has already been exploited, and CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day with a deadline of this Friday for federal agencies.

The bug is a heap-based buffer overflow reachable through OAuth traffic. It scores 9.8 under CVSS 3.1 (9.3 under 4.0) and needs no credentials. The trigger is crafted traffic sent to a virtual server that has both an APM access policy and an OAuth authorization server profile attached.

That configuration detail matters, so read it carefully. If you use APM only as an OAuth client or resource server, F5 says you aren't affected. If you've set it up to issue tokens, you are.

Affected versions are 17.1.0 through 17.1.3, 17.5.0 through 17.5.1, and 21.1.0. The fixes are engineering hotfixes for now: Hotfix-BIGIP-17.1.3.5.0.41.14-ENG, Hotfix-BIGIP-17.5.1.9.0.160.12-ENG and Hotfix-BIGIP-21.1.0.2.0.30.22-ENG. If you can't take a hotfix today, F5 Support has an iRule mitigation you can put on the affected virtual servers.

Here's the part that should worry network teams most. Locking down the management interface, which is the standard advice after every BIG-IP scare of the last five years, does nothing here. The vulnerable code path lives on the data plane, on the same virtual servers users log in through. Shadowserver counts more than 14,000 BIG-IP APM instances reachable on the internet, though it can't say how many have OAuth server profiles configured.

F5's advisory and CISA's entry are both silent on who is exploiting this and how many systems have been hit. For detection, the pattern F5 describes is a burst of failed OAuth authentications and odd commands followed shortly by a TMM SIGABRT. A TMM crash on an APM box this week deserves a look, not a restart and a shrug.

Given that a nation-state crew walked off with BIG-IP source code and undisclosed vulnerability details from F5 last year, a pre-auth data-plane bug showing up already weaponized isn't a shock. Inventory your OAuth server profiles, apply the hotfix or the iRule, and check the logs back to at least early September.
